DATE:
20090202

SUPERIOR
COURT OF JUSTICE -
ONTARIO

RE:
R.
v. B. B.

BEFORE:
Justice
Spies

COUNSEL:

Julie
Battersby
, for the Crown

Uma Kancharla
, for
B. B.

DATE HEARD:
January 29 and 30, 2009

Subject to any further Order by a court of competent
jurisdiction, an Order has been made in this proceeding directing that the
identity of the complainant and any information that could disclose such identity
shall not be published in any document or broadcast in any way.

RULING ON CROWN APPLICATION TO INTRODUCE AFTER-THE-FACT CONDUCT AND DEFENCE
APPLICATION CONCERNING PRIVILEGE

Introduction

[
1
]

Ms. Battersby on behalf of the Crown,
brought an application for an order admitting into evidence certain after-the-fact
conduct of Mr. B. concerning his interaction with Rabbi Berman on August 13,
2007, and further interaction with Simon Kalkstein, the supervisor at the Bloor
and Spadina offices of Jewish Family and Child Services (JFCS) on or about
August 13, 2007. Ms. Kancharla, counsel for Mr. B., brought a cross-application
to exclude this evidence on the basis that statements made by Mr. B. to these
two gentlemen were privileged and that, in any event, the evidence ought not to
be admitted.

[
2
]

Ms. Kancharla’s position is that the
communications between Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman were religious communications
and that the communications he had with Mr. Kalkstein were in his capacity as a
counsellor for JFCS. The only case provided by counsel on the issue of
privilege was
R. v. Gruenke
,
[1]
a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada dealing
with religious communications. There was no dispute that the privileges claimed
are not
prima facie
privileged at common law or subject to “class”
privilege, and that the evidence is, therefore, not
prima facie
inadmissible.
The Court
in
Gruenke

held that religious communications and I presume by
analogy, communications for the purpose of family counselling, might be
excluded in particular cases where the
Wigmore
criteria are satisfied.
The Court also set out the procedure to be followed.
[2]

[
3
]

I heard evidence as part of a blended
voir
dire.
Both Rabbi Berman and Mr. Kalkstein were called by Ms. Battersby. Ms.
Kancharla had filed an affidavit sworn by Mr. B. setting up his claim that the
communications were made in confidence, but making no reference to any of the
details about his meeting with either Rabbi Berman or Mr. Kalkstein. Ms.
Kancharla seemed to assume that the cross-examination of Mr. B. would be
limited to the four corners of the affidavit, but when she inquired about that,
I informed her that he could be asked other questions, including questions
about the statements he was alleged to have made, provided they were relevant
to the issue of privilege. Ms. Kancharla then decided not to file Mr. B.’s affidavit
after all.

Issues

[
4
]

The onus is on Ms. Kancharla to satisfy
me that the communications should be excluded from evidence on the basis of privilege
[3]
and if not, the burden is on Ms.
Battersby to persuade me that this evidence is admissible as after-the-fact
conduct. If the communications are found to be privileged, some of the other
conduct could still be admissible as after-the-fact conduct without breaching
the privilege.

[
5
]

The issues that I must, therefore,
consider are:

(a)

Are the
communications between Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman privleged as religious
communications?

(b)

Subject to my ruling
on privilege, is all or some of the evidence concerning the interaction between
Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman admissible as after-the-fact conduct?

(c)

Are the
communications between Mr. B. and Mr. Kalkstein privileged?

(d)

Subject to my ruling
on privilege, is all or some of the evidence concerning the interaction between
Mr. B. and Mr. Kalkstein admissible as after-the-fact conduct?

Analysis

Are the communications between Mr.
B. and Rabbi Berman privleged as religious communications?

[
6
]

Rabbi Berman
testified that on August 13, 2007, a gentleman attended at Shaar Shalom
Synagogue and asked to speak to a Rabbi. He was available and so he had a
conversation with this gentleman who he identified as Mr. B., although he could
not recall his name. He had never seen Mr. B. before and had had no dealings
with his family. He met with Mr. B. in his office with the door closed in the
synagogue. He acknowledged that he offers advice and that when someone comes to
him, it is implicit that the conversation will be confidential. There was no
discussion with Mr. B. as to whether or not their conversation would be
confidential.

[
7
]

Mr. B. told him that
he wanted to speak to a Rabbi, that he had marital problems with his wife, that
they had had some kind of argument and that he had hit her; he believed that Mr.
B. said that this had happened a couple of days before. Mr. B. also asked him
questions about how he could have faith in God, and about how to pray to God. Rabbi
Berman assumed that Mr. B. was there for advice or counselling and he asked him
if he had had any counselling. Mr. B. told him that he had had counselling with
a particular person at JFCS. Rabbi Berman called JFCS but only got that
person’s voicemail. He then called another of the JFCS offices. The person at
that office told him that Mr. B. was on the news and was wanted by police and
considered armed and dangerous and that he would call the police.  Rabbi Berman
told Mr. B. this and told him that he should turn himself in. Mr. B. became
agitated, said that he could not trust anyone and ran away, although Rabbi
Berman said he might have remained for as long as five minutes. Rabbi Berman
then called police and when they arrived, he assumed he told the officer what
had happened, including the nature of his conversation with Mr. B., but was not
sure. He did do so for certain a few months later when he received a call from
a police officer about the incident.

[
8
]

Rabbi Berman testified that people do
come to him for advice with their difficulties in life and that although he
generally does not share information, there is no religious dictate that any
communications be kept confidential. He can share information in certain
circumstances, if, for example, public safety issues arise, as saving a life
precedes everything else in Jewish law. Rabbi Berman felt that was the case
here, given he had been told Mr. B. was armed and dangerous, and he did not
think he was breaching any confidence when he spoke to police. He has only
broken this confidence on one other occasion. Rabbi Berman explained as well
that there was no confessional concept to what he was doing and that in Judaism
you do not confess to a Rabbi. He did not feel that his decision to speak to
police impinged on his duties as a Rabbi.

[
9
]

In light of this evidence, I will
consider the four
Wigmore
criteria as directed by the court
in
Gruenke
.

Ms. Kancharla must satisfy me on all four of these criteria on a balance
of probability. Before considering the first criterion, however, I note that
Ms. Battersby does not dispute that the communication between Mr. B. and Rabbi
Berman at least falls into the religious communications category, I presume
because the discussion took place in a synagogue and Mr. B. did ask questions
about God and prayer.

[
10
]

Turning then to the
first
Wigmore
criterion; did the communication originate in a confidence
that it would not be disclosed? The Supreme Court
stated in
Gruenke

that
it is absolutely crucial that the communications originate with an expectation
of confidentiality as that is the raison d’
ê
tre
of the privilege.
[4]
Although Ms. Gruenke testified at
the preliminary hearing, the Court concluded that there was no evidence that
she made the statements to a pastor and a counsellor in the confident belief
that they would be disclosed to no one and that although confidentiality was a
desired aspect of the relationship, it was not essential.
[5]

Ms. Battersby submitted that it was fatal in this case that I had no evidence
from Mr. B. that he expected the conversation to be kept confidential. As Ms.
Kancharla pointed out, however, I do have the evidence of Rabbi Berman that
that was implicit. The discussion took place in his office behind closed doors,
in a holy place, and included questions by Mr. B. about religion. His comment
to Rabbi Berman after he was told that the police had been called about not
trusting anyone is some suggestion that he expected confidentiality although I
have no evidence as to his religious beliefs or what he, in fact, expected on
that issue. The fact that Judaism does not include a confessional aspect is not
dispositive as
in
Gruenke
, Lamer C. J., speaking for the majority, held
that the absence of a formal practice of confessions was not in and of itself
determinative. However, in the absence of evidence from Mr. B., and given there
was no discussion about keeping the conversation confidential, I find that the communications
between Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman do not satisfy the first
Wigmore

criterion, particularly given the particular circumstances that caused Rabbi
Berman to believe that the safety of others was at risk. In the event I am
wrong, I will go on to consider the other criteria.

[
11
]

Turning to the second

Wigmore
criterion; the issue is whether or not the element of
confidentiality is essential to the full and satisfactory maintenance of the
relation between
the parties
. The decision of the majority
in
Gruenke

provides no further guidance as in that case the Court did not have to
consider the other
Wigmore
criteria. I do find guidance, however, from
the minority decision of Madam Justice L’Heureux-Dubé, who concurred in the
result, but provided her own comments on the “religious communications”
privilege issue. She stated on this point that the privacy interests of the
religious leader and individual involved, in combination with the benefit to society
of the relationship’s confidentiality, will not be sufficient to pass the
second criteria in every case and that determination of this issue will
involve, among other things, a consideration of the nature of the particular
relationship at bar.
[6]
Again, apart from the fact Mr. B.
asked some questions about prayer and God, it is difficult to determine in the
absence of any evidence from him as to whether or not he went to Rabbi Berman
for religious counselling. Even if I make that assumption, it is clear from the
evidence of Rabbi Berman that from his perspective confidentiality was not
essential. Although he testified it was implicit and I would assume desired, he
was of the view that an exception applied in the circumstances of this case. He
had no difficulty in telling the police about the conversation. This is not a
case where someone like a Rabbi has come to court and refused or resisted
advising the court of what would otherwise be a confidential communication. In
fact, Rabbi Berman talked to police voluntarily and told them about the
conversation and he testified that his disclosure of this information to police
did not impinge on his duties as a Rabbi. In my view, the Defence cannot satisfy
the second criteria.

[
12
]

As for the third
Wigmore

criterion, the relation must be one which, in the opinion of the community,
ought to be sedulously fostered. Although the Court
in
Gruenke

concluded
that for policy reasons, religious communications do not give rise to a
prima
facie
privilege in the same way as solicitor-client communications, the
Court did find that a case-by-case analysis would allow the courts to determine
in a particular case whether an individual’s freedom of religion would be
imperilled by the admission of the evidence as guaranteed by section 2(a) of
the
Charter
and implicitly recognized that confidential religious
communications ought to be fostered
.
Even if I were to assume that the
primary purpose in Mr. B. going to see Rabbi Berman was for religious counselling
or guidance, given the evidence of Rabbi Berman, given that Mr. B. disclosed
evidence of a crime and there was a legitimate concern in the mind of Rabbi
Berman for the safety of others, there could be no universal expectation of
confidentiality in this specific relationship. The Defence cannot make out the
third
Wigmore
criterion.

[
13
]

As for the fourth and final
Wigmore

criterion; I must consider whether the injury that would inure to the relation
by the disclosure of the communications is greater than the benefit thereby
gained for the correct disposal of litigation. There could be no doubt that the
Defence cannot make out this final factor. Rabbi Berman voluntarily disclosed
the information that the Crown seeks to lead as evidence at trial and had no
concerns that his decision to do so would adversely impact on his duties as a
Rabbi. As for the benefit to be gained, if the evidence is admissible as after-the-fact
conduct, it clearly has probative value and would amount to an admission of
certain important facts if the jury concludes on all the evidence that Mr. B.
was talking about an argument with his wife on August 11, 2007, the date of the
alleged sexual assault.

[
14
]

For all of these reasons, I find that the
communications between Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman should not be excluded from
evidence on the grounds of privilege and their admission into evidence will not
infringe Mr. B.’s freedom of religion.

Is all or some of the evidence
concerning the interaction between Mr. B. and Rabbi Berman admissible as after-the-fact
conduct?

[
15
]

Ms. Battersby submits that the evidence
of Rabbi Berman is relevant because of the admission made by Mr. B. that he hit
his wife and the fact he fled when he was told that the police had been called.
Ms. Kancharla argued that this statement should not be admitted because Mr. B.
only admitted to Rabbi Berman that he hit his wife and that
the principles in
R.
v. Arcangioli
[7]

should apply to exclude this
evidence. I understand from Ms. Battersby, however, that the complainant will
testify that she was forcibly confined over a prolonged period of time and that
during that time, in addition to the alleged sexual assault, Mr. B. did hit her
and threaten her with a knife. He is charged with assault with a weapon, namely
a knife, in addition to the charge of sexual assault and other offences.

[
16
]

As the Supreme Court
stated in
R. v.
White
,
[8]

Arcangioli
stands for the
proposition that a piece of evidence should not be put to the jury unless it is
relevant to the determination of a live issue in this case. Where the conduct
may be equally explained by reference to “consciousness of guilt” of two or
more offences and the accused has admitted to one, the evidence has no
probative value with respect to any particular offence.
[9]

If the jury finds that Mr. B. admitted to Rabbi Berman that he hit his wife and
that this admission relates to the day of the alleged sexual assault, that
evidence is relevant to the charge of assault with a weapon and may, as well, corroborate
some of the complainant’s anticipated evidence. This evidence may also be
relevant to any defence put forward. Similarly, the fact Mr. B. fled when
advised the police had been called may also be relevant to the issue of guilt
although his flight is consistent with an admission that he hit his wife and
probably has no probative value on the other offences charged unless the extent
of his flight could be considered out of all proportion to an admission that he
hit his wife.
[10]
What instructions I ultimately
give the jury will depend on all of the evidence that is led, but certainly at
this stage I could not conclude that this evidence would have no probative
value and should not be heard by the jury.

[
17
]

Ms. Kancharla submitted that this
evidence will be prejudicial, in the sense that it hurts Mr. B.’s position, but,
of course, that is not the type of prejudice that is relevant to admissibility.
I find that the probative value of this evidence is not outweighed by any
possible prejudice to Mr. B. which, in any event, I will be able to deal with
in my instructions to the jury.

[
18
]

For these reasons, I find that the
evidence of Rabbi Berman is admissible as after-the-fact conduct of Mr. B..

Are the communications between Mr. B. and Mr. Kalkstein
privileged?

[
19
]

Simon Kalkstein is a long term employee
of JFCS and currently the supervisor at its Bloor and Spadina office. He had
never met Mr. B. before but identified him as someone he met with at his office
when he dropped in. Although he did not testify to a specific date, counsel
agreed that it was on or about August 13, 2007. Mr. Kalkstein thought the
meeting was around 9:30 a.m.. When Mr. B. arrived at the office, he told Mr.
Kalkstein that he had no money and that he was hungry. He explained that he had
had some trouble with his wife and complained that the social work profession
sided with women over men. In his evidence-in-chief, Mr. Kalkstein testified that
Mr. B. told him that he had threatened his wife and that he wanted to consult
with a lawyer who would take Legal Aid. Mr. Kalkstein thought this was a fairly
recent event. In cross-examination, Mr. Kalkstein admitted that he told police
that Mr. B. had said something “along the lines of ‘I threatened her’,” a
reference to his wife, and that that was why he gave him the name of a criminal
lawyer.  He stated that this is what he thought Mr. B. said. Mr. B. was quite
respectful and said that he wanted to do the right thing and wanted legal
advice first. Mr. Kalkstein gave him the names of two criminal lawyers, $20 and
a food voucher and sent him on his way.

[
20
]

About ten minutes after Mr. B. left,
coincidentally, Mr. Kalkstein mentioned that he had seen him to the Director of
Finance of JFCS who told him that he was wanted by police and that Mr.
Kalkstein should call them, which he did. He believes that  officers attended
around noon. Some time later, he was contacted again and gave a signed
statement. He testified that he had no difficulty telling the police about his
conversation with Mr. B. and felt no sense of confidentiality although he
admitted that one would generally assume that what he was told would be kept
confidential. He thought that because Mr. B. was wanted by police that he was
obliged to give them any helpful information and that he needed to co-operate.

[
21
]

Mr. Kalkstein testified that as a social
service agency it is not unusual for people to drop in. They have a large
clientele of people who come in for counselling on a regular basis. He did not
suggest that as a supervisor he saw anyone on a regular basis but testified that
he did see people who came in on a drop in basis if he was available. He did
not know if Mr. B. had had any prior contact with the agency and he did not
check the database to find out. There was no discussion between them as to
whether or not their conversation would be confidential and no discussion of Mr.
B. coming back. He did speak to Mr. B. again the next day when he called and he
gave him the name of another criminal lawyer. No further details of this
conversation were provided.

[
22
]

In light of this evidence, I will
consider again the four
Wigmore
criteria as directed by the court
in
Gruenke
.

With respect to Mr. Kalkstein, the absence of evidence from Mr. B., in my
view, is fatal. There is no evidence that Mr. Kalkstein is a counsellor and
based on the nature of the conversation, the only advice Mr. B. asked for was
the name of a lawyer, which, in the circumstances, Mr. Kalkstein interpreted as
a criminal lawyer. Mr. Kalkstein was not his counsellor and there is no
suggestion that he was going to enter into a counselling relationship with Mr.
B.. Although Mr. Kalkstein would normally keep such a communication
confidential, and the conversation was in private, there is absolutely no
evidence that Mr. B. believed, or had reason to believe, that the conversation
was intended to be kept confidential. I could not even conclude on the evidence
before me that confidentiality was a desired aspect of the relationship.

[
23
]

Again, in the event I am wrong, I will go
on to consider the other criteria. Turning to the second
Wigmore

criterion; the issue is whether or not the element of confidentiality is
essential to the full and satisfactory maintenance of the relation between the
parties. There is no evidence to suggest, based on the questions asked, that Mr.
B. went to see Mr. Kalkstein for any kind of counselling. The purpose of his
visit was to deal with his need for cash and food and for the name of a lawyer.
This is corroborated by the fact that Mr. Kalkstein had no difficulty in
telling the police about the conversation. He did not suggest that he would
have any difficulty in repeating his evidence in this trial. Although Mr.
Kalkstein may have felt the need to cooperate with police, the fact remains
that he talked to them voluntarily and disclosed his conversation with Mr. B..
In my view, the Defence cannot satisfy the second criterion.

[
24
]

As for the third
Wigmore

criterion, the relation must be one, which in the opinion of the community,
ought to be sedulously fostered. Although a counselling relationship would
arguably be such a relationship, that is not the nature of the relationship
here between Mr. Kalkstein and Mr. B.. This was simply a drop in visit for some
emergency help. Again the Defence cannot make out the third criterion.

[
25
]

As for the fourth and final
Wigmore

criterion; I must consider whether the injury that would inure to the relation
by the disclosure of the communications is greater than the benefit thereby
gained for the correct disposal of litigation. There could be no doubt that the
Defence cannot make out this final factor. Mr. Kalkstein voluntarily disclosed
the information that the Crown seeks to lead as evidence at trial and had no
concerns about doing so. Given my views on the third
Wigmore
criterion,
there is no injury to any relationship that deserves the protection of a
privilege claim. As for the benefit to be gained, presuming that the evidence
is admissible as after-the-fact conduct, it clearly has probative value.
Although Mr. Kalkstein has some uncertainty about what exactly Mr. B. said,
that is an issue for the jury. If the jury finds that Mr. B. admitted
threatening his wife, depending on the issue of timing that could amount to an
admission of one of the elements of one of the charges before the court, namely
threatening the death of his wife on August 11, 2007, the date of the alleged
sexual assault.

[
26
]

For all of these reasons, I find that the
communications between Mr. B. and Simon Kalkstein are not excluded from
evidence on the ground of privilege.

Is all or some of the evidence
concerning the interaction between Mr. B. and Mr. Kalkstein admissible as after-the-fact
conduct?

[
27
]

As I have already said, if the jury finds
that Mr. B. admitted threatening his wife, depending on the issue of timing,
that could amount to an admission of an element of one of the charges before
the court, namely threatening death of his wife on August 11, 2007, the date of
the alleged sexual assault. Whether or not he made this admission will be a
factual issue for the jury to determine. Ms. Battersby also argues that the
jury can draw an inference from the fact that Mr. B. was looking for a criminal
lawyer. On this point, I note that Mr. Kalkstein did not give this evidence,
only that based on what Mr. B. told him, he assumed that was the kind of lawyer
that he needed. Finally, Ms. Battersby relies on the fact that Mr. B. had not
yet surrendered to police. The relevance of this aspect of the evidence,
however, presumes that he saw Mr. Kalkstein after Rabbi Berman which is likely
from what I know but not necessarily so. The fact Mr. B. was looking for a
lawyer may be more problematic but at this stage I could not conclude that his
request for a name has no probative value. Even if it is possible he thought he
was asking for a family lawyer, that would be for the jury to decide. His
request for the names of some lawyers is part of the same conversation where Mr.
B. explains why he wants the name of the lawyer. In my view, the evidence
should be heard by the jury and, as with the evidence of Rabbi Berman, what
instructions I ultimately give the jury will depend on all of the evidence that
is led including the significance, if any, of the fact that Mr. B. had not yet
turned himself into police.

Disposition

[
28
]

For all of these
reasons, the Crown’s application to introduce after-the-fact conduct is granted
and the Defence application seeking to exclude the evidence on the ground of privilege
is dismissed. However, as the full extent of the inferences that the jury could
draw from the post-offence evidence can only be determined after all of the
evidence is heard, counsel should be careful about what they say about this
anticipated

evidence in their opening statements to avoid any chance of my having to
contradict them in my final instructions to the jury. A pre-charge conference
on this issue will be held before closing addresses so that further submissions
can be made as to how I should instruct the jury on these issues.
